  3. Promax differs from varimax in that it
    1. lets the factors correlate
    2. fits the data better
    3. changes the unique variances
    4. needs more factors
  4. How many angles does a turn of three factors have?
    1. one
    2. two
    3. three
    4. six
  5. To find the verbal and the mathematical factor, factanal() needs to be told
    1. which tests are verbal and which are mathematics tests
    2. only the scores and the number of factors: the groups show up in the correlations
    3. the correlation between the two factors
    4. the names of the factors
Answers 1 a. 2 b. 3 a. 4 c. 5 b.

6.7 Factor scores

6.7.1 Parameters, but not shocks

So far the chapter has estimated the parameters of the model, the loadings and the unique variances. With three or more critics, the covariance matrix pins them down (Section 6.3). The shocks are another matter: the quality of each restaurant, and the quirks behind each rating.

In the earlier chapters, the parameters gave the shocks for free. There, \(\mathbf x_t=A\boldsymbol\varepsilon_t\) had as many shocks as variables, so \(A\) was square. Once \(A\) was chosen, it could be undone, \(\boldsymbol\varepsilon_t=A^{-1}\mathbf x_t\), and every shock followed exactly from the data. The PCA scores \(\mathbf f_t=\Gamma'\mathbf x_t\) are an example (Section 4.2). Whether a matrix can be undone depends on its shape:

  • More rows than columns, that is, more variables than shocks. Then \(A\) can still be undone, as long as no column is a combination of the others: the matrix \((A'A)^{-1}A'\) does it, because \((A'A)^{-1}A'A=I\). If the four critics had no quirks, for example, each rating would be \(x_{ti}=\lambda_if_t\), \(A\) would be the single column \((\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_4)'\), and any one rating would reveal the quality exactly, \(f_t=x_{ti}/\lambda_i\).
  • More columns than rows, that is, more shocks than variables. Then no matrix undoes \(A\), because different shocks produce the same data.

The factor model is of the second kind. Its \(A=\begin{pmatrix}\Lambda&\Psi^{1/2}\end{pmatrix}\) has \(p\) rows and \(k+p\) columns (Section 6.2). The four critics give four ratings, but there are five shocks: the quality and the four quirks. Whatever quality a restaurant has, the quirks can make up the difference. For any value of \(f_t\), the quirks \(u_{ti}=x_{ti}-\lambda_if_t\) reproduce the four ratings exactly. The left panel shows this for one restaurant: pick any quality on the horizontal axis, and the four lines give the quirks the critics would have needed that evening.

f2 <- function(x, d = 2) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d)

crit_weights <- function(m) { l <- crit_lam[1:m]; p <- crit_psi[1:m]; (l / p) / (1 + sum(l^2 / p)) }

fig_crit_anyquality <- function(t = crit_pick) {
  x <- crit_X[t, ]; tau <- sum(crit_lam^2 / crit_psi)
  f_hat <- sum(crit_weights(4) * x); sd_f <- sqrt(1 / (1 + tau)); f_true <- crit_d$quality[t]
  fs <- seq(-1.5, 3.5, length.out = 401)
  cols <- setNames(c(col_a1, col_a2, col_third, "#16a085"), crit_names)
  quirks <- purrr::map_dfr(1:4, function(i) tibble(f = fs, u = x[i] - crit_lam[i] * fs, critic = crit_names[i]))
  ends <- quirks |> group_by(critic) |> slice_tail(n = 1) |> ungroup() |> arrange(u)
  for (j in 2:nrow(ends)) ends$u[j] <- max(ends$u[j], ends$u[j - 1] + 0.3)   # keep the labels apart
  p1 <- ggplot(quirks, aes(f, u, colour = critic)) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey70") +
    annotate("text", x = -1.5, y = 0.12, label = "no quirk", hjust = 0, vjust = 0, size = 3.4, colour = "grey45") +
    geom_line(linewidth = 1.1) +
    geom_text(data = ends, aes(label = critic), hjust = 0, nudge_x = 0.08, size = 3.6, show.legend = FALSE) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = cols, guide = "none") +
    scale_x_continuous(limits = c(-1.5, 4.4), breaks = -1:3) +
    labs(title = "Every quality fits the four ratings",
         subtitle = "the quirk each critic would need, for each quality",
         x = "quality of the restaurant", y = "quirk needed")
  dens <- tibble(f = fs, d = dnorm(fs, f_hat, sd_f))
  top <- max(dens$d)
  p2 <- ggplot(dens, aes(f, d)) +
    geom_area(fill = col_f, alpha = 0.2) + geom_line(colour = col_f, linewidth = 1.1) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = f_hat, colour = col_f, linetype = "22") +
    geom_vline(xintercept = f_true, colour = "#2c3e50") +
    annotate("text", x = f_hat + 0.08, y = top * 1.08, hjust = 0, size = 3.7, colour = col_f,
             label = sprintf("factor score %s", f2(f_hat))) +
    annotate("text", x = f_true - 0.08, y = top * 1.08, hjust = 1, size = 3.7, colour = "#2c3e50",
             label = sprintf("true quality %s", f2(f_true))) +
    scale_x_continuous(limits = c(-1.5, 3.5), breaks = -1:3) +
    scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, top * 1.15), expand = c(0, 0)) +
    labs(title = "But some qualities are more plausible",
         subtitle = "how likely each quality is, with the quirks it needs",
         x = "quality of the restaurant", y = "plausibility (density)")
  p1 + p2
}

# draw the figure
fig_crit_anyquality()

So the ratings never pin down a restaurant’s quality. They only make some values more plausible than others, because large quirks are unlikely. The right panel weighs each quality by how likely it is, together with the quirks it needs (with normal shocks). The plausible qualities form a bell curve. Its peak is not where the four quirks average zero, for two reasons: a quirk counts more against a quality when it belongs to a critic whose quirks are usually small, and a quality far above the average restaurant is itself unlikely. The next subsection finds the peak. The true quality, which we know only because the data are simulated, lies inside the curve but not at its centre.

In a factor model the parameters are identified, but the shocks are not: \(A\) has more columns than rows, so it has no inverse. The factors can only be estimated, and the estimates are called factor scores.

6.7.2 Estimating quality from four ratings

Here is the idea for one factor and the four critics, with the loadings and unique variances of the model. It finds the centre of the bell curve.

  1. Each critic’s rating, divided by her loading, measures the quality with an error: \[x_{ti}/\lambda_i=f_t+u_{ti}/\lambda_i .\] The error has variance \(\psi_i/\lambda_i^2\), which is small for a critic with a large loading and small quirks.
  2. Average the four measurements, and give each a weight proportional to its precision \(\lambda_i^2/\psi_i\), one over its error variance. These weights make the error of the average as small as possible. With the total precision \(\tau=\sum_i\lambda_i^2/\psi_i\) (tau), the average is \[\hat f^{\,B}_t=\frac1\tau\sum_i\frac{\lambda_i^2}{\psi_i}\cdot\frac{x_{ti}}{\lambda_i}=\frac1\tau\sum_i\frac{\lambda_i}{\psi_i}\,x_{ti}.\] Its error, \(\frac1\tau\sum_i(\lambda_i/\psi_i)\,u_{ti}\), has variance \(\frac1{\tau^2}\sum_i(\lambda_i^2/\psi_i^2)\,\psi_i=1/\tau\). This is Bartlett’s score (Bartlett 1937), hence the \(B\).
  3. \(\hat f^{\,B}_t\) is quality plus an error, and quality has variance one, so \(\operatorname{Var}(\hat f^{\,B}_t)=1+1/\tau\). The regression of quality on \(\hat f^{\,B}_t\) has the slope \(\operatorname{Cov}(f_t,\hat f^{\,B}_t)/\operatorname{Var}(\hat f^{\,B}_t)=1/(1+1/\tau)=\tau/(1+\tau)\), so the best prediction of quality shrinks \(\hat f^{\,B}_t\) towards zero, the average quality: \[\hat f_t=\frac{\tau}{1+\tau}\,\hat f^{\,B}_t=\sum_i w_i\,x_{ti},\qquad w_i=\frac{\lambda_i/\psi_i}{1+\tau}.\] This is the regression score, the centre of the bell curve in the figure above.

The weights of the four critics are 0.15, 0.36, 0.08 and 0.43. Critic 4 counts most (loading 0.90, quirk variance 0.19) and critic 3 least (0.60 and 0.64). With \(k\) factors the same idea gives \(\hat{\mathbf f}_t=\Lambda'\Sigma^{-1}\mathbf x_t\), the regression of the factors on the variables: its coefficients are \(\Sigma^{-1}\operatorname{Cov}(\mathbf x_t,\mathbf f_t)\), the matrix version of a covariance over a variance, and \(\operatorname{Cov}(\mathbf x_t,\mathbf f_t)=\operatorname{Cov}(\Lambda\mathbf f_t+\mathbf u_t,\mathbf f_t)=\Lambda\). (With correlated factors, \(\operatorname{Cov}(\mathbf x_t,\mathbf f_t)=\Lambda\Phi\), and the scores become \(\hat{\mathbf f}_t=\Phi\Lambda'\Sigma^{-1}\mathbf x_t\).)

The scores do not depend on the units (Section 6.5.4). With critic 1 on the 100-point scale, her loading is ten times and her unique variance a hundred times as large. So her precision \(\lambda_1^2/\psi_1\) and the total precision \(\tau\) stay the same, and her weight \(w_1=(\lambda_1/\psi_1)/(1+\tau)\) becomes ten times smaller. That exactly offsets her ten times larger rating, and every restaurant gets the same score as before: the scores estimate the same quality \(f_t\). With \(k\) factors, \(\Lambda'\Sigma^{-1}\) becomes \(\Lambda'\Sigma^{-1}\operatorname{diag}(\alpha)^{-1}\), with the same effect.

6.7.3 The scores are never exact

How well do the scores track the true quality? The regression score is Bartlett’s score times a number, so both have the same squared correlation with quality:

\[ \rho^2=\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(f_t,\hat f^{\,B}_t)^2}{\operatorname{Var}(f_t)\operatorname{Var}(\hat f^{\,B}_t)} =\frac{1}{1+1/\tau}=\frac{\tau}{1+\tau} . \]

With critic 1 alone, \(\rho^2=0.56\), her communality. Each further critic adds her precision to \(\tau\) and moves \(\rho^2\) towards one:

crit_weights <- function(m) { l <- crit_lam[1:m]; p <- crit_psi[1:m]; (l / p) / (1 + sum(l^2 / p)) }

crit_reliability <- function(m) { tau <- sum(crit_lam[1:m]^2 / crit_psi[1:m]); tau / (1 + tau) }

f2 <- function(x, d = 2) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d)

fig_crit_scores <- function() {
  d <- purrr::map_dfr(1:4, function(m) {
    lab <- sprintf("%s\nρ² = %s", c("critic 1 alone", "critics 1 and 2", "critics 1 to 3", "all four critics")[m],
                   f2(crit_reliability(m)))
    tibble(est = drop(crit_X[, 1:m, drop = FALSE] %*% crit_weights(m)), true = crit_d$quality, panel = lab)
  }) |> mutate(panel = factor(panel, levels = unique(panel)))
  ggplot(d, aes(est, true)) + geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, colour = col_f, linetype = "22") +
    geom_point(alpha = 0.35, size = 1.2, colour = "#2c3e50") +
    facet_wrap(~ panel, nrow = 1) + coord_equal(xlim = c(-3, 3), ylim = c(-3, 3)) +
    labs(x = "estimated quality (factor score)", y = "true quality") +
    theme(strip.text = element_text(size = 11, face = "bold"))
}

# draw the figure
fig_crit_scores()

Even with all four critics, \(\rho^2=0.91\), not one: a restaurant with good ratings may simply have caught its critics on good evenings. More critics push \(\rho^2\) closer to one, but never all the way. This is factor indeterminacy: with more shocks than variables, the data never pin down the factors exactly (Section 6.7.1). Everitt and Hothorn (Section 5.8) consider it a more damaging problem than the rotation.

In practice the loadings and unique variances are estimated, and factanal() computes the scores from the estimates:

crit_fs <- factanal(crit_X, factors = 1, scores = "regression")
head(round(crit_fs$scores, 2), 3)            # the first three restaurants
##      Factor1
## [1,]   -0.40
## [2,]   -0.02
## [3,]    0.54
cor(crit_fs$scores, crit_d$quality)^2        # how well the scores track the true quality
##              [,1]
## Factor1 0.8863885

The estimated scores track the simulated quality with a squared correlation of 0.89, close to the 0.91 of the model. scores = "Bartlett" gives Bartlett’s scores instead. With one factor they are the regression scores times \((1+\tau)/\tau\), so they track quality equally well.

Check your understanding
  1. In the regression score, a critic’s weight is proportional to
    1. her loading
    2. her loading divided by her unique variance
    3. the variance of her ratings
    4. one, the same for every critic
  2. Even with all four critics, the scores track quality with \(\rho^2=0.91\), because
    1. the sample is small
    2. there are more shocks than ratings, so quality and quirks cannot be fully separated
    3. the loadings were estimated
    4. the model is wrong
  3. Unlike factor scores, PCA scores
    1. are exact functions of the data
    2. have variance one
    3. are always positive
    4. need a rotation
  4. In \(\mathbf x_t=A\boldsymbol\varepsilon_t\), the shocks can be computed exactly from the data when \(A\)
    1. has more columns than rows
    2. is square and invertible, or has more rows than columns and no column is a combination of the others
    3. has a diagonal block
    4. never
Answers 1 b. 2 b. 3 a. 4 b.

6.8 The US states

The simulated critics and test scores were built to fit a factor model. Real data need not. Take the six state indicators of Chapter 2, with the 50 states as observations: income, illiteracy, life expectancy, the murder rate, the high-school graduation rate and the number of days with frost.

X <- state.x77[, c("Income", "Illiteracy", "Life Exp", "Murder", "HS Grad", "Frost")]
factanal(X, factors = 1)$PVAL                 # one factor
##    objective 
## 3.872699e-07
fa2 <- factanal(X, factors = 2)               # two factors, varimax
fa2$PVAL
##    objective 
## 0.0004735598
print(fa2$loadings, cutoff = 0)
## 
## Loadings:
##            Factor1 Factor2
## Income      0.141   0.683 
## Illiteracy -0.644  -0.500 
## Life Exp    0.744   0.332 
## Murder     -0.989  -0.133 
## HS Grad     0.381   0.833 
## Frost       0.513   0.237 
## 
##                Factor1 Factor2
## SS loadings      2.373   1.594
## Proportion Var   0.396   0.266
## Cumulative Var   0.396   0.661
round(fa2$uniquenesses, 3)
##     Income Illiteracy   Life Exp     Murder    HS Grad      Frost 
##      0.514      0.336      0.336      0.005      0.161      0.681

One factor loads 0.48 on income, -0.89 on illiteracy, 0.74 on life expectancy, -0.81 on murder, 0.72 on graduation and 0.63 on frost: a general factor, much like the well-being index of the first principal component (Section 4.5). But the test rejects it (statistic 47.0 on 9 degrees of freedom, p-value below 0.0001). Two factors are rejected as well (20.1 on 4 degrees of freedom, p-value of 0.0005). Three factors leave no degrees of freedom (Section 6.4). Here they happen to reproduce the correlations exactly, so nothing is left to test. This is common with real data. The model is an approximation, and the test finds the gap.

Here are the two varimax factors all the same, as a description, next to the first two principal components of the same six indicators (Section 4.5). The components come from the correlation matrix, as in Chapter 4, because the indicators are measured in different units; the factors need no such choice (Section 6.5.4). Both panels show loadings (Section 4.2.5): the arrow of an indicator has as its coordinates how far one standard deviation of the first and of the second component, or factor, moves the standardised indicator. An arrow that reached the dashed circle would have all of its variance in the plane.

loading_panel <- function(L, pos, col, title, subtitle, what) {
  d <- tibble(var = rownames(L), x = L[, 1], y = L[, 2]) |> left_join(pos, by = "var")
  circ <- tibble(t = seq(0, 2 * pi, length.out = 200), x = cos(t), y = sin(t))
  ggplot() + axes0 +
    geom_path(data = circ, aes(x, y), colour = "#dddddd", linetype = "22") +
    geom_segment(data = d, aes(0, 0, xend = x, yend = y), colour = col, linewidth = 1,
                 arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.2, "cm"), type = "closed")) +
    geom_text(data = d, aes(x + dx, y + dy, label = var, hjust = hj, vjust = vj), size = 3.7, colour = "#2c3e50") +
    coord_equal(xlim = c(-1.2, 1.2), ylim = c(-1.2, 1.2)) +
    labs(title = title, subtitle = subtitle, x = paste("loading on", what, "1"), y = paste("loading on", what, "2")) +
    theme(plot.title = element_text(colour = col, face = "bold"))
}

fig_states_pca_fa <- function() {
  # where each label goes, relative to its arrow's tip: offset (dx, dy) and alignment (hj, vj)
  pos_pca <- tribble(~var,        ~dx,   ~dy,   ~hj, ~vj,
                     "Income",     0.03,  0.05,  0,   0,
                     "Illiteracy", 0,    -0.07,  0.5, 1,
                     "LifeExp",    0.05,  0,     0,   0.5,
                     "Murder",     0,     0.06,  0.5, 0,
                     "HSGrad",     0.05,  0.02,  0,   0.5,
                     "Frost",      0.04, -0.05,  0,   1)
  pos_fa  <- tribble(~var,        ~dx,   ~dy,   ~hj, ~vj,
                     "Income",    -0.04,  0.04,  1,   0.5,
                     "Illiteracy", 0,    -0.07,  0.5, 1,
                     "LifeExp",    0.06,  0.03,  0,   0.5,
                     "Murder",     0,    -0.07,  0.5, 1,
                     "HSGrad",     0,     0.07,  0.5, 0,
                     "Frost",      0.05, -0.08,  0,   1)
  loading_panel(st_pca_A, pos_pca, col_third, "PCA", "two components, correlation matrix", "component") +
    loading_panel(st_L, pos_fa, col_f, "Factor analysis", "two factors, turned by varimax", "factor")
}

# draw the figure
fig_states_pca_fa()

In the right panel, the first factor is dominated by the murder rate (loading -0.99), with life expectancy (0.74), illiteracy (-0.64) and frost (0.51). The second factor is graduation (0.83) and income (0.68), with illiteracy (-0.50). The uniqueness of murder is 0.005, the smallest value that factanal() allows: the estimate has hit the boundary, a Heywood case (Section 6.3.3). With a lower bound of 0.0001 instead (control = list(lower = 0.0001)), the estimate drops to 0.0001 as well. The first factor is then almost the murder rate itself, and the other variables load on it through their correlations with murder.

In the left panel, the first component contrasts illiteracy and murder with life expectancy, graduation, frost and income, and the second is mainly income. The two fans of arrows are much alike, but turned against each other: varimax has picked the turn that puts one axis through murder and the other through graduation and income. Neither description is more true than the other, since both summarise the same correlations. The arrows have different lengths, though, and Section 6.9 shows what the lengths mean. Given the rejected tests and the Heywood case, these two factors are a description, not a discovery. Everitt and Hothorn (Section 5.9) show two real examples that fit better: life expectancies by country, age and sex, and drug use by American college students.

Check your understanding
  1. For the states, the test of two factors gives a p-value of 0.0005, and three factors have no degrees of freedom. So
    1. two factors fit well
    2. the test rejects two factors, and with three factors nothing is left to test
    3. the test rejects three factors
    4. one factor fits
  2. The uniqueness of murder, 0.005, means that
    1. murder is unrelated to the factors
    2. the estimate hit the boundary: the first factor is almost the murder rate itself
    3. murder has the smallest variance of the six indicators
    4. the model fits perfectly
Answers 1 b. 2 b.

6.9 Factor analysis and PCA

Both methods describe many variables by a few, and with small unique variances they give similar answers (Everitt and Hothorn, Section 5.10). But they are different models:

PCA Factor analysis
Shocks \(p\), as many as variables \(k\) common factors and \(p\) unique shocks
Restriction on \(A\) perpendicular arrows, ordered by length each unique shock moves one variable
What it explains the variances the covariances
A change of units changes the components rescales the loadings and unique variances, but not the factors (maximum likelihood)
Scores exact, \(\mathbf f_t=\Gamma'\mathbf x_t\) estimated, never exact
One more component or factor the first ones stay the same all factors can change
A test of the model none yes, if \(\text{df}>0\)

The states of Section 6.8 show these differences at work, starting with the second-to-last row. With one factor, the loadings of income, illiteracy, life expectancy, murder, graduation and frost are 0.48, -0.89, 0.74, -0.81, 0.72 and 0.63. The first column of the two-factor solution as estimated, before varimax, is different: 0.24, -0.71, 0.79, -1.00, 0.51 and 0.54. The first principal component has the loadings 0.59, -0.89, 0.79, -0.83, 0.81 and 0.66, whether one component is kept or two.

The biggest difference is in what counts as common. Each indicator is standardised, so its variance is one, and each method splits this variance in two parts:

  • PCA: the part that its first two components keep, and the rest, which the other four components carry.
  • Factor analysis: the part that the two factors explain, the communality, and the unique variance, which belongs to the indicator alone.

The bars show the two splits for each indicator. Each coloured part is split once more, into the first component or factor (dark) and the second (light). These are the squared loadings, and their total is the squared length of the indicator’s arrow in Section 6.8. Turning the factors, for instance by varimax, moves the line between the dark and the light part, but not the total, so the totals at the end of the bars do not depend on the turn.

pct <- function(x, d = 0) paste0(formatC(100 * x, format = "f", digits = d), "%")

fig_fa_pca <- function() {
  light <- function(col) grDevices::colorRampPalette(c(col, "white"))(5)[3]
  fills <- c(pca1 = col_third, pca2 = light(col_third), fa1 = col_f, fa2 = light(col_f), rest = "#e6e6e6")
  labs_m <- c(pca1 = "PCA: first component", pca2 = "PCA: second component",
              fa1 = "factor analysis: first factor (varimax)", fa2 = "factor analysis: second factor (varimax)",
              rest = "the rest of the indicator's variance")
  ord <- st_share$var[order(st_share$fa, decreasing = TRUE)]     # bottom to top: the largest unique variance on top
  pos <- tibble(var = ord, y = seq_along(ord))
  w <- 0.36                                                      # height of each bar; PCA above, factor analysis below
  bars <- st_share |> left_join(pos, by = "var") |>
    tidyr::pivot_longer(c(pca1, pca2, fa1, fa2), names_to = "part", values_to = "share") |>
    mutate(method = substr(part, 1, nchar(part) - 1), yc = ifelse(method == "pca", y + 0.2, y - 0.2)) |>
    group_by(var, method) |> mutate(x0 = cumsum(share) - share, x1 = cumsum(share)) |> ungroup()
  tots <- bars |> group_by(var, method, yc) |> summarise(total = sum(share), .groups = "drop") |>
    mutate(lab = ifelse(total > 0.99, pct(total, 1), pct(total)))
  ggplot() +
    geom_rect(data = distinct(bars, var, method, yc), aes(xmin = 0, xmax = 1, ymin = yc - w / 2, ymax = yc + w / 2,
                                                         fill = "rest")) +
    geom_rect(data = bars, aes(xmin = x0, xmax = x1, ymin = yc - w / 2, ymax = yc + w / 2, fill = part)) +
    geom_text(data = tots, aes(x = total, y = yc, label = lab, colour = method), hjust = -0.15, size = 3.9,
              fontface = "bold", show.legend = FALSE) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = fills, labels = labs_m, breaks = names(labs_m), name = NULL) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = c(pca = col_third, fa = col_f)) +
    scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent, breaks = seq(0, 1, 0.25), limits = c(0, 1.1), expand = c(0, 0)) +
    scale_y_continuous(breaks = pos$y, labels = pos$var, expand = c(0.02, 0.02)) +
    guides(fill = guide_legend(ncol = 2, byrow = TRUE)) +
    labs(x = "share of the indicator's variance", y = NULL) +
    theme(legend.position = "top", panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(), panel.grid.minor.y = element_blank())
}

# draw the figure
fig_fa_pca()

Together, the two components keep 76% of the total variance of the six indicators, and the two factors explain 66%. The difference is largest for frost and income, the indicators with the largest unique variances (0.68 and 0.51). PCA keeps 60% of the variance of frost and 86% of that of income, while the factor model counts only 32% and 49% as common. PCA looks for the directions of largest variance, and part of an indicator’s unique variance lies along them, so the components take it in. Factor analysis sets it apart. For graduation and life expectancy the factor model claims a little more than PCA, and for murder almost all of the variance, because of the Heywood case.

With real data, the true common parts are unknown. In the simulated six tests, where they are known, PCA claims too much for every test: two principal components keep between 58% and 74% of each test’s variance, while the true common parts lie between 36% and 64%. And both methods are pointless if the variables are almost uncorrelated, because then there is nothing in common to find.

Check your understanding
  1. For frost, two principal components keep 60% of the variance and two factors explain 32%, because
    1. the components also take in part of the unique variance of frost
    2. frost is the most reliable indicator
    3. PCA uses the covariance matrix
    4. the factor model ignores frost
  2. Which of the two methods can be tested against the data?
    1. PCA
    2. factor analysis, when the model has positive degrees of freedom
    3. both
    4. neither
Answers 1 a. 2 b.

6.10 Summary

  • A factor model writes each variable as loadings times a few common factors, plus a unique shock: \(x_{ti}=\lambda_{i1}f_{t1}+\dots+\lambda_{ik}f_{tk}+u_{ti}\), or \(\mathbf x_t=\Lambda\mathbf f_t+\mathbf u_t\), so that \(\Sigma=\Lambda\Lambda'+\Psi\). Only the common factors create covariance. In the structural form \(\mathbf x_t=A\boldsymbol\varepsilon_t\) it has \(k+p\) shocks, and the unique shocks fill a diagonal block of \(A\).
  • With one factor, two variables fix only the product of their loadings. A third variable pins the loadings down (just identified), and a fourth adds two testable restrictions, the tetrad conditions. In general the model has \(\text{df}=\tfrac12\big[(p-k)^2-(p+k)\big]\) restrictions.
  • A negative or zero unique variance is a Heywood case: the model does not fit, or the sample is too small.
  • Maximum likelihood finds the \(\Lambda\Lambda'+\Psi\) closest to \(S\), and the likelihood ratio test asks whether the remaining gap is more than sampling noise. A change of units rescales the loadings and unique variances, and leaves the factors, the fit and the test as they were (scale invariance).
  • With two or more factors, the factors can be turned without changing the fit. Varimax picks the turn with the simplest structure, and promax also lets the factors correlate. Rotation changes the description, not the fit. The data find the groups of variables, such as the verbal and the mathematics tests, but the names of the factors come from what we know about the variables.
  • Here the data choose the turn, so the analysis is exploratory. Theory can instead fix loadings in advance, for example a zero where a test should not depend on an ability. That makes it confirmatory (Chapter 8).
  • The parameters are identified, but the shocks are not: \(A\) has more columns than rows, so it has no inverse. Factor scores estimate the factors. Each variable counts in proportion to its loading over its unique variance, and the scores are never exact (factor indeterminacy).
  • For the states, the tests reject one and two factors, and two factors give a Heywood case. A factor model is an approximation, and its factors are interpretations.
  • PCA explains the variances and mixes the unique variances into its components. Factor analysis explains the covariances and sets the unique variances apart.

A factor model explains the covariances by a few common factors, and keeps each variable’s own noise apart.

6.10.1 Further reading

  • Everitt and Hothorn (2011), An Introduction to Applied Multivariate Analysis with R, Chapter 5: Spearman’s example and the Heywood case, scale invariance, principal factor and maximum likelihood estimation, the test for the number of factors, rotation, factor scores, two examples (life expectancies, and drug use by American college students), and the comparison with PCA.
  • Spearman (1904), “General intelligence, objectively determined and measured”, the origin of the one-factor model.
  • Thurstone (1947), Multiple Factor Analysis, on several factors and simple structure.
  • Kaiser (1958) on varimax, and Hendrickson and White (1964) on promax.
  • Lawley and Maxwell (1971), Factor Analysis as a Statistical Method, on maximum likelihood and the test.
  • Bartholomew, Knott and Moustaki (2011), Latent Variable Models and Factor Analysis: A Unified Approach, a modern treatment that includes factor scores.
